content: Cefaclor is a cephalosporin-type antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections, including those affecting the middle ear, skin, urinary tract, and respiratory tract. It is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold or flu. Dosage and Administration: Capsules: Administer 250-500 mg orally every 8 hours for infections such as lower respiratory tract infections, otitis media, skin infections, and urinary tract infections caused by susceptible bacteria. Extended-release tablets: Administer 375 mg orally every 12 hours for 7-10 days for skin infections or 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days for acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis. Pharyngitis and tonsillitis: Use 250-500 mg orally every 8 hours or 750 mg extended-release tablets every 12 hours for 10 days. Renal or hepatic impairment: No specific dosage adjustments are provided, but reduced renal function should be considered, and careful monitoring is advised. Important Considerations: Beta-lactamase-negative, ampicillin-resistant strains of Haemophilus influenzae should be considered resistant to cefaclor, even if in vitro susceptibility is observed. For beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections, therapy should last at least 10 days. Avoid prescribing cefaclor in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection to reduce the risk of drug-resistant bacteria. Drug Interactions: Vaccines: Cefaclor decreases the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines (e.g., BCG, cholera, typhoid) due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is complete. Aminoglycosides (e.g., amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin): Cefaclor may increase nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. Hormonal contraceptives: Cefaclor may reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives by altering intestinal flora. Additional or alternative birth control methods may be advisable. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., atezolizumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab): Cefaclor may interfere with their therapeutic effects. Use caution and monitor. Probenecid: Cefaclor levels may increase due to competition for renal tubular clearance. Monitor closely. Other antibiotics (e.g., chloramphenicol): May antagonize cefaclor’s effects. Use caution. Side Effects: Common side effects include diarrhea (3%), elevated liver enzymes (3%), eosinophilia (2%), moniliasis (2%), vaginitis (2%), and rash (1-2%). Rare but serious side effects include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pseudomembranous colitis, anemia, neutropenia, jaundice, and hypersensitivity reactions. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to superinfections, such as oral thrush or vaginal yeast infections. Special Populations: Pregnancy: Use only if necessary, as adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. Animal studies are not always predictive of human response. Nursing mothers: The effect on nursing infants is unknown; exercise caution. Renal impairment: Dosage should be reduced by half if creatinine clearance is 10-30 mL/min and by three-quarters if clearance is <10 mL/min to avoid central nervous system toxicity. Storage and Preparation: Store capsules, extended-release tablets, and dry powder for suspension at 20-25°C (68-77°F). Reconstituted oral suspension should be refrigerated and used within 14 days. Shake oral suspension well before use. Extended-release tablets should not be chewed, crushed, or split and should be taken with or within 1 hour of food. Additional Notes: Cefaclor is excreted primarily in the urine (60-80% unchanged). Hemodialysis shortens the half-life of cefaclor by 25-30%. Patients should complete the full prescribed course of therapy, even if symptoms improve, to prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria. This medication has been prescribed because the benefits outweigh the risks. However, careful monitoring is essential, especially in patients with renal impairment or those taking interacting medications.
